screens.title: DNS Client Configuration & Resolution
screens.narratorSegment: DNS turns human names into IP addresses so your systems can communicate. In this lesson you will learn the role of the DNS resolver, how a Linux client specifies which DNS servers to use, and the practical tools to inspect and fix name resolution. We’ll look at the traditional /etc/resolv. conf file and why modern systems often manage it dynamically through NetworkManager or systemd-resolved. You will also see concrete command-line examples using host, dig and nslookup for forward and reverse lookups, and learn how DNS caching can produce stale results and how to clear it. Through short, focused tasks you’ll practice configuring persistent DNS using distribution tools and diagnosing common mistakes like unreachable nameservers or firewall blocking. By the end you’ll be able to verify that your VM resolves names correctly and identify whether a DNS problem is local, upstream, or a cached artifact. Consider how reliable name resolution impacts every service on a server — from SSH to package updates.

screens.title: What DNS is and what a resolver does
screens.narratorSegment: DNS is a distributed naming database that maps human-friendly domain names to IP addresses so devices can find each other on a network. A DNS resolver acts on behalf of a client system: when an application requests a name, the resolver takes that query and either answers from cache or queries authoritative servers until an answer is retrieved. For example, when you open a browser to reach google. com, your resolver may first check a local cache, then ask your configured nameserver, which will navigate the DNS hierarchy to find the domain’s authoritative server. A common misconception is that the resolver is always the same as the nameserver listed in /etc/resolv. conf; in many environments the nameserver is a recursively resolving service provided by an ISP or a public DNS provider. Why this matters: understanding this chain helps you decide whether a failure is local, on the configured nameserver, or at an authoritative server. Takeaway: think of the resolver as your system’s guide through the DNS hierarchy and test with targeted queries to see where resolution stops. What DNS is and what a resolver does means a resolver accepts the client's query, consults cache or other servers, and returns an ip address or an error.. In practical terms, definition, responsibilities, and a concrete example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
What DNS is and what a resolver does
DNS maps names to IPs. The resolver orchestrates queries across servers and caches answers to speed future requests.
Definition
A resolver processes client name queries, consults cache or other DNS servers, and returns answers or errors.
Concrete example
Browser requests google.com; resolver checks cache, queries configured nameserver, and the nameserver walks the DNS hierarchy to the authoritative server.
Common misconception
Assuming the configured nameserver is authoritative for all names. Often it is a recursive resolver that queries other servers.
Key Takeaway

Treat the resolver as a client-side service that may be cached locally or provided by an upstream server; use targeted queries to find where resolution stops.

Resolver flow (annotated cards)
Application request
An app asks the resolver to resolve a hostname.
Cache check
Resolver returns cached answer if recent; otherwise it queries nameserver.
Upstream lookup
Configured nameserver performs recursive lookup through authority chain and returns the IP.
Quick check example
# Quick forward lookup with host
host google.com

# Quick reverse lookup with host
host 172.217.160.142

screens.title: /etc/resolv.conf: Structure and directives
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/resolv. conf file is the primary legacy location where a Linux client lists resolver settings. Two common directives appear there: nameserver and search. A nameserver directive provides the IP address of a DNS server the client can query. You can list multiple nameserver lines; the client will try them in order until one responds. The search directive lists domain suffixes appended to short hostnames; for example, with search example. com, resolving server1 will try server1. example. com. A typical file may include a header from NetworkManager; on modern systems this file may be a symlink or generated automatically. A practical example: a resolv. conf containing nameserver 8.8.8.8 and nameserver 8.8.4.4 uses Google’s public DNS servers as resolvers. A misconception is that editing resolv. conf directly always makes persistent changes; on systems using NetworkManager or systemd-resolved, manual edits can be overwritten. Takeaway: inspect resolv. conf first, but change persistent DNS using the distribution’s recommended method. /etc/resolv.conf: Structure and directives means nameserver entries list resolver ips; search defines suffixes for unqualified names. check how the file is managed before editing.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
/etc/resolv.conf: Structure and directives
Understand nameserver and search directives and recognize dynamic generation markers.
nameserver
Specifies the IP address of a DNS server to query. Multiple entries are tried in order.
search
Adds domain suffixes to short hostnames to form FQDNs for resolution attempts.
Warning
On systems with NetworkManager or systemd-resolved, this file may be overwritten. Use the distro tools for persistent changes.
Key Takeaway

Check whether /etc/resolv.conf is a symlink or contains a generator comment before editing to avoid losing your changes.

resolv.conf example
# Generated by NetworkManager search example.com nameserver 8.8.8.8 nameserver 8.8.4.4
  • Try order: If 8.8.8.8 does not respond, the client tries 8.8.4.4.
  • Search usage: ping webserver becomes webserver.example.com when search is set.
  • Persistence: Edit via nmcli or netplan when resolv.conf is managed automatically.
Quick check
Run cat /etc/resolv.conf to inspect current resolver entries and any generator comments.

screens.title: How resolv.conf is managed: NetworkManager vs systemd-resolved
screens.narratorSegment: Modern Linux distributions may not leave /etc/resolv. conf as a static file you edit directly. NetworkManager can generate resolv. conf from connection settings and systemd-resolved often provides a local stub resolver and manages a symlink to a generated file. The correct approach is to use the distribution tool for persistent changes: with NetworkManager use nmcli or nmtui to set ipv4. dns on the connection, and with systemd-resolved change /etc/systemd/resolved. conf or use resolvectl to set DNS and then restart the service. For example, using nmcli you modify the connection's ipv4. dns and then bring the connection up. A common mistake is editing /etc/resolv. conf directly, then seeing changes disappear after a network restart. A practical verification step is to run resolvectl status on systems with systemd-resolved or to check the connection configuration in nmcli to ensure the configured servers are present. Takeaway: make changes where the distro persists them, not to the generated file. How resolv.conf is managed: NetworkManager vs systemd-resolved means persistent dns must be configured with the tool that manages resolv.conf on your distribution to avoid overwritten edits.. In practical terms, when to edit the file directly and when to use distribution tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
resolv.conf: NetworkManager vs systemd-resolved
Follow the managed configuration path for persistent DNS changes to avoid being overwritten.
NetworkManager flow
Configure DNS with nmcli connection modify & bring the connection up; NetworkManager regenerates resolv.conf from the connection policy.
systemd-resolved flow
systemd-resolved may provide a stub resolver and a symlinked resolv.conf; configure resolv.conf via /etc/systemd/resolved.conf or resolvectl.
Common pitfall
Editing the generated file directly will be reverted. Always identify the manager and use its configuration facility.
Example commands
# NetworkManager
sudo nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection up my-eth0

# systemd-resolved
# Edit /etc/systemd/resolved.conf and restart
sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved
resolvectl status
Checklist to avoid overwritten edits
  • Run ls -l /etc/resolv.conf to see if it is a symlink or has generator comments.
  • Check for systemd-resolved with resolvectl status or for NetworkManager with nmcli connection show.
  • Make persistent changes through the responsible manager, then verify resolv.conf content.
Pro Tip

If you must test quickly, temporarily edit resolv.conf, but document and then make the persistent change using the manager to avoid surprises.

screens.title: Configuring DNS with nmcli (NetworkManager)
screens.narratorSegment: When NetworkManager manages your connection, the correct way to make persistent DNS changes is through its connection configuration. Use nmcli to list connections, modify the connection's ipv4. dns field with space-separated IPs, and then bring the connection up to apply the change. For example, identify your primary connection name with nmcli connection show, then run nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1" and activate it with nmcli connection up. Afterward, verify the change with cat /etc/resolv. conf and by performing a forward lookup with host or dig to ensure resolution now uses the intended servers. A common misconception is that restarting NetworkManager or the network interface is unnecessary — applying the connection is required for the new DNS settings to take effect. Takeaway: changes via nmcli are reproducible and survive service restarts because they are stored in the connection profile. Configuring DNS with nmcli (NetworkManager) means always modify the networkmanager connection profile for persistent dns instead of editing the generated resolv.conf.. In practical terms, a reproducible method to persist dns on nm-managed systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process
Configuring DNS with nmcli
Use nmcli to make persistent DNS changes in the NetworkManager connection profile.
# Show connections
nmcli connection show

# Modify DNS for your connection (replace name)
sudo nmcli connection modify my-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1"

# Apply the change
sudo nmcli connection up my-eth0

# Verify
cat /etc/resolv.conf
host www.example.com
  • Identify the connection name to avoid changing the wrong profile.
  • Provide IPs separated by spaces inside quotes for nmcli.
  • Verify by querying names using host or dig and checking /etc/resolv.conf content.
Scenario & pitfalls

If you edit /etc/resolv.conf directly and NetworkManager manages it, your edits will disappear on the next connection update. Always make the change in the connection profile and then bring the connection up.

Check your work

Confirm the nameserver IPs appear in /etc/resolv.conf and that forward lookups succeed using host or dig.

screens.title: Configuring DNS with Netplan / systemd-resolved
screens.narratorSegment: On systems using Netplan and systemd-resolved, add nameserver addresses under the nameservers section of the Netplan YAML for your interface, and then apply the configuration. After applying netplan changes, use resolvectl status to inspect the current DNS servers recognized by systemd-resolved. Alternatively, configure /etc/systemd/resolved. conf to set DNS and FallbackDNS and then restart systemd-resolved. A concrete example is adding addresses: [8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1] under your interface and running sudo netplan apply. A common misconception is that editing Netplan YAML requires only a simple copy-paste; YAML is whitespace-sensitive so indentation must be correct. Also be aware that resolv. conf may point to a systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53, in which case resolvectl is the right tool to inspect or flush caches. Takeaway: use Netplan or resolvectl on these systems and always verify with resolvectl status and a forward lookup. Configuring DNS with Netplan / systemd-resolved means add nameservers to netplan yaml or resolved.conf and verify with resolvectl; watch yaml indentation carefully.. In practical terms, persistent dns on ubuntu and systemd-resolved-managed systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Netplan + systemd-resolved
keyIdea.text: Add nameservers to Netplan YAML or resolved.conf and verify with resolvectl; watch YAML indentation carefully.

content.html:
Process
Netplan and systemd-resolved configuration
Edit Netplan YAML or resolved.conf for persistent DNS on Ubuntu-style systems and verify with resolvectl.
# Example Netplan fragment
ethernets:
  enp0s3:
    dhcp4: no
    addresses: [192.168.1.100/24]
    gateway4: 192.168.1.1
    nameservers:
      addresses: [8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1]

# Apply
sudo netplan apply

# Verify with systemd-resolved
resolvectl status
  • Ensure YAML indentation is correct; a malformed file will fail to apply.
  • If resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.53, use resolvectl to inspect the resolver state.
Common checks
  • After applying netplan, run resolvectl status to confirm the DNS servers systemd-resolved will use.
  • If needed, edit /etc/systemd/resolved.conf and restart systemd-resolved to set global options.
Pro Tip

When testing, query a known public server directly with dig at to separate local configuration issues from upstream server problems.

screens.title: Using host for forward and reverse lookups
screens.narratorSegment: The host command is a lightweight utility for performing forward and reverse DNS lookups. For a forward lookup you run host followed by the domain name and it prints the resolved IP. For reverse lookups you provide an IP and host will return the PTR record if available. Host’s output is concise and easy to read, making it useful for quick verification. For example, running host google. com returns the A record address, while running host 172.217.160.142 returns a pointer to a host name. One misconception is relying on host alone to troubleshoot authority issues; host doesn’t show the full DNS message sections like dig does. Use host for a fast sanity check, then use dig to dig deeper into authority or timing. Takeaway: start with host for quick answers, and escalate diagnostic depth when you need authority or timing details. Using host for forward and reverse lookups means use host for simple forward and reverse lookups; switch to dig for more detailed diagnostic information.. In practical terms, simple, readable outputs for quick checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Using host for forward and reverse lookups
host is ideal for quick verification of name-to-IP and IP-to-name mappings.
# Forward lookup example
host google.com
# Output: google.com has address 172.217.160.142

# Reverse lookup example
host 172.217.160.142
# Output includes the PTR record
  • Use host when you want a compact human-readable result quickly.
  • When you require authority or additional sections, switch to dig for full details.
Example scenario

If a service performs a reverse lookup for a connecting IP, use host on that IP to ensure the PTR record exists and points to the expected hostname. If it does not, mail servers or security checks may fail the connection.

Quick Check

Run host on both the hostname and its resolved IP to verify forward and reverse mappings match expected values.

screens.title: Using dig for deep DNS inspection
screens.narratorSegment: dig, the Domain Information Groper, is the go-to tool for detailed DNS diagnostics. Unlike host, dig shows the full DNS response structure including question, answer, authority, and additional sections, plus query timing and the server that answered. Use dig to request specific record types, for example dig google. com MX to view mail exchange records, or dig @8.8.8.8 google. com to query a particular DNS server and bypass your configured resolvers. A concrete example: if your configured nameserver fails to resolve a name but a public server succeeds, using dig at different servers quickly reveals where the discrepancy lies. A common misconception is interpreting the absence of an answer as a server outage; sometimes the server intentionally returns no records or the zone lacks the requested type. Takeaway: use dig to compare answers from different servers and inspect the authority section to find which server is definitive for a domain. Using dig for deep DNS inspection means use dig to request specific record types and to compare responses from different dns servers to isolate where resolution fails.. In practical terms, answer, authority, additional sections and querying specific servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.text: Use dig to request specific record types and to compare responses from different DNS servers to isolate where resolution fails.

content.html:
Core Tool
Using dig for deep DNS inspection
dig shows full DNS response sections and lets you target specific servers and record types.
# Basic lookup
dig google.com

# Query specific record type
dig google.com MX

# Query a specific server
dig @8.8.8.8 google.com
  • Compare answers from your configured server and a known public server to isolate issues.
  • Read the authority section to identify the authoritative server for a zone.
Practical example

If dig against your nameserver returns SERVFAIL but dig against 8.8.8.8 returns an answer, your upstream nameserver is the likely problem. Fix or replace it in resolv.conf or the manager.

Check Your Understanding

After a change, run dig against both the configured nameserver and a public server to confirm the new configuration is used and that the authoritative server returns the expected records.

screens.title: nslookup vs dig vs host
screens.narratorSegment: host, dig and nslookup overlap but each fits different needs. host is compact and human-friendly, ideal for fast forward and reverse checks. dig is detailed and preferred for diagnostics because it exposes the full DNS message and lets you target specific servers and record types. nslookup provides interactive mode and is familiar across platforms, but it is generally less verbose than dig and is not the preferred tool for advanced diagnostics. For example, use host when you want a quick mapping, use dig when you need to see the authority and additional sections or measure query time, and use nslookup for a simple interactive session when you prefer that style. A common mistake is relying only on one tool; always confirm suspicious results with a second tool and by querying a known reliable nameserver. content.html:
Comparison
nslookup vs dig vs host
Select the tool based on verbosity and diagnostic needs.
host
Concise, human-friendly forward and reverse lookups for quick verification.
dig
Full DNS message, record type queries, and server targeting for deep diagnostics.
nslookup
Interactive mode and familiar cross-platform behavior, useful for iterative queries.
Practical advice
  • Confirm results by querying a known public server with dig to separate local configuration issues from upstream problems.
  • Use multiple tools when troubleshooting: a quick host check followed by dig gives both speed and depth.
Key Takeaway

No single tool solves every DNS problem; combine quick checks with deep inspection to find where resolution fails.

screens.title: DNS caching and clearing stale entries
screens.narratorSegment: DNS caching improves performance by avoiding repeated network queries for recent answers, but caches can become stale after a DNS record changes. On modern Linux systems systemd-resolved maintains a cache you can inspect with resolvectl statistics and clear with resolvectl flush-caches. Other caching daemons include dnsmasq or nscd; in those cases restarting the respective service clears the cache. For instance, sudo resolvectl flush-caches forces systemd-resolved to drop cached entries, ensuring subsequent lookups fetch current records. A common troubleshooting sequence is to verify network connectivity to a nameserver, perform a direct dig against a known good server, and if that shows the updated record while local responses show the old one, flush the local cache. A misconception is that flushing cache always fixes resolution; sometimes caches exist upstream or the authoritative server’s TTL has not expired. Takeaway: use cache flushing as a targeted tool after confirming that authoritative servers already serve the updated record. DNS caching and clearing stale entries means flush local caches only after confirming authoritative servers host the expected records; use resolvectl for systemd-resolved.. In practical terms, why caches exist, how to inspect them, and how to flush them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
DNS caching and clearing stale entries
Inspect and clear caches carefully to address stale resolution without masking other issues.
# systemd-resolved: view stats
resolvectl statistics

# systemd-resolved: flush
sudo resolvectl flush-caches

# nscd: restart to clear cache
sudo systemctl restart nscd

# Verify after flush
dig www.example.com
  • Confirm that authoritative servers already return the updated record before flushing caches.
  • Understand the caching daemon used on your system so you use the correct flush method.
Troubleshooting flow
  1. Verify network connectivity to nameservers with ping.
  2. Query authoritative or public servers with dig to confirm the correct record.
  3. Flush the local resolver cache and re-query to see if the change propagates.
Key Takeaway

Flushing is a valid fix for stale local caches, but always confirm upstream state first to avoid chasing the wrong problem.

screens.title: Hands-on lab: configure and verify DNS, then troubleshoot
screens.narratorSegment: This practical walkthrough ties together configuration and diagnostics. Start by checking the current resolvers: run cat /etc/resolv. conf to see nameserver and search directives. If NetworkManager manages your connection, use nmcli connection show to find the profile name and then sudo nmcli connection modify ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1" followed by sudo nmcli connection up. On Netplan systems, edit the YAML to add nameserver addresses and run sudo netplan apply. After applying changes verify with cat /etc/resolv. conf and resolvectl status. Next, perform forward lookups with host and dig, and do a reverse lookup on any returned IP with host to confirm PTR records. If you see inconsistent results across servers, query a known public server with dig @9.9.9.9 to separate local from upstream problems. If your system still shows an old IP, flush local caches with sudo resolvectl flush-caches or restart nscd. Finally, practice the assessment scenario: if dig @192.168.1.254 fails but dig @8.8.8.8 succeeds, update your configured nameserver to a reliable server and verify resolution. Takeaway: follow this checklist to configure, verify, and troubleshoot DNS reliably. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Configure and verify DNS, then troubleshoot
Follow these steps to make changes safely and confirm they work.
Step 1 — Inspect
Run cat /etc/resolv.conf and ls -l /etc/resolv.conf to see if it is managed or a symlink.
Step 2 — Configure persistently
Use nmcli for NetworkManager or edit Netplan YAML for systemd-resolved systems and apply the change.
Step 3 — Verify lookups
Use host and dig, and query a public server like 9.9.9.9 if results differ to isolate the issue.
Step 4 — Flush cache
If you see stale records, run sudo resolvectl flush-caches or restart the caching daemon and re-check.
Scenario practice

If dig @192.168.1.254 fails but dig @8.8.8.8 succeeds, the local configured nameserver is likely broken. Update your resolver configuration to a known good server and verify resolution again.

fullNarratorScript:
DNS turns human names into IP addresses so your systems can communicate. In this lesson you will learn the role of the DNS resolver, how a Linux client specifies which DNS servers to use, and the practical tools to inspect and fix name resolution. We’ll look at the traditional /etc/resolv. conf file and why modern systems often manage it dynamically through NetworkManager or systemd-resolved. You will also see concrete command-line examples using host, dig and nslookup for forward and reverse lookups, and learn how DNS caching can produce stale results and how to clear it. Through short, focused tasks you’ll practice configuring persistent DNS using distribution tools and diagnosing common mistakes like unreachable nameservers or firewall blocking. By the end you’ll be able to verify that your VM resolves names correctly and identify whether a DNS problem is local, upstream, or a cached artifact. Consider how reliable name resolution impacts every service on a server — from SSH to package updates.

These objectives focus on foundational knowledge and initial configuration skills. First, you will learn the role of DNS and what a resolver does in client-server name resolution. This understanding helps you judge whether a problem is DNS-related or a broader network issue. Second, you'll learn how to inspect and edit the DNS client configuration found at /etc/resolv. conf, and why some distributions generate that file dynamically. The practical outcome is being able to identify the configured nameservers and search suffixes. Third, you'll use the host command for quick forward and reverse lookups. It is compact and great for quick checks. Finally, you will practice using dig and nslookup for deeper inspection and for targeting specific name servers. Each objective includes a short two-sentence skill description and a verified competency milestone you can check after performing the commands on a workstation.

These objectives extend configuration into real troubleshooting and service-specific checks. You will learn how modern services like NetworkManager or systemd-resolved often generate resolv. conf and the safe ways to make persistent changes through nmcli or resolvectl. You will practice clearing DNS cache using systemd-resolved commands or restarting cache daemons like nscd when present. You will also learn to differentiate forward and reverse lookups, why reverse DNS can affect mail delivery, and how the /etc/hosts file overrides DNS. Finally, you will apply all skills in a hands-on troubleshooting scenario where you diagnose a misconfigured nameserver and verify your fix with targeted dig queries. Each card describes the skill and why it matters, plus a simple mnemonic or small visual cue to help you remember the corrective action paths. Learning Objectives — Part 2 means make persistent configuration changes with the distribution tools and verify by querying a known good dns server before declaring success.. In practical terms, advanced checks, caching, and troubleshooting skills. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DNS is a distributed naming database that maps human-friendly domain names to IP addresses so devices can find each other on a network. A DNS resolver acts on behalf of a client system: when an application requests a name, the resolver takes that query and either answers from cache or queries authoritative servers until an answer is retrieved. For example, when you open a browser to reach google. com, your resolver may first check a local cache, then ask your configured nameserver, which will navigate the DNS hierarchy to find the domain’s authoritative server. A common misconception is that the resolver is always the same as the nameserver listed in /etc/resolv. conf; in many environments the nameserver is a recursively resolving service provided by an ISP or a public DNS provider. Why this matters: understanding this chain helps you decide whether a failure is local, on the configured nameserver, or at an authoritative server. Takeaway: think of the resolver as your system’s guide through the DNS hierarchy and test with targeted queries to see where resolution stops. What DNS is and what a resolver does means a resolver accepts the client's query, consults cache or other servers, and returns an ip address or an error.. In practical terms, definition, responsibilities, and a concrete example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The /etc/resolv. conf file is the primary legacy location where a Linux client lists resolver settings. Two common directives appear there: nameserver and search. A nameserver directive provides the IP address of a DNS server the client can query. You can list multiple nameserver lines; the client will try them in order until one responds. The search directive lists domain suffixes appended to short hostnames; for example, with search example. com, resolving server1 will try server1. example. com. A typical file may include a header from NetworkManager; on modern systems this file may be a symlink or generated automatically. A practical example: a resolv. conf containing nameserver 8.8.8.8 and nameserver 8.8.4.4 uses Google’s public DNS servers as resolvers. A misconception is that editing resolv. conf directly always makes persistent changes; on systems using NetworkManager or systemd-resolved, manual edits can be overwritten. Takeaway: inspect resolv. conf first, but change persistent DNS using the distribution’s recommended method. /etc/resolv.conf: Structure and directives means nameserver entries list resolver ips; search defines suffixes for unqualified names. check how the file is managed before editing.. In practical terms, nameserver and search explained with examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Modern Linux distributions may not leave /etc/resolv. conf as a static file you edit directly. NetworkManager can generate resolv. conf from connection settings and systemd-resolved often provides a local stub resolver and manages a symlink to a generated file. The correct approach is to use the distribution tool for persistent changes: with NetworkManager use nmcli or nmtui to set ipv4. dns on the connection, and with systemd-resolved change /etc/systemd/resolved. conf or use resolvectl to set DNS and then restart the service. For example, using nmcli you modify the connection's ipv4. dns and then bring the connection up. A common mistake is editing /etc/resolv. conf directly, then seeing changes disappear after a network restart. A practical verification step is to run resolvectl status on systems with systemd-resolved or to check the connection configuration in nmcli to ensure the configured servers are present. DNS caching improves performance by avoiding repeated network queries for recent answers, but caches can become stale after a DNS record changes. On modern Linux systems systemd-resolved maintains a cache you can inspect with resolvectl statistics and clear with resolvectl flush-caches.
